title: Merryshins and the Mighty Dewdrop
markdown:
Aeridor was a kingdom unlike any map would quite admit, a land of cloud-brushed peaks where towers of sky-stone kissed the heavens and deep valleys hung like forgotten silken scarves between wind-swept ridgelines. The very air hummed with gentle magic. Dawn painted the clouds in hues of warm buttery light. In a cozy cave lined with soft emerald moss that smelled of damp earth and ancient secrets, Merryshins awoke. He was an ogre, quite large, and larger still in gentleness. Skin the colour of a sun-dappled forest floor; eyes like polished river pebbles. Today he wanted a day free of heroic volunteering. Pine shadows on a mountain path. No fetching of lost thunderclaps. No untangling of sky-serpent kites.

“Just one day,” he rumbled, stones in a slow stream. “No runaway rainbows. No disputes between grumpy cloud-herders. Ordinariness.”

He ambled out of his cave, the first rays of dawn stretching across the sky, warming his moss-green skin. He was just settling onto his favourite sun-warmed rock, a perfect perch for observing the world without being part of it, when a frantic flutter disturbed the morning calm. It was elf Nessa, a whirlwind of iridescent wings, her face etched with a worry that seemed to dim her usual sparkle.

Nessa’s voice, usually like the tinkling of tiny silver bells, was laced with urgency. She landed lightly on his broad shoulder, dewdrop-coloured wings shimmering. “Merryshins. Thank the wind spirits for your stillness.”

Merryshins sighed, a sound like the wind rustling through a hollow log. “Good morning, Nessa. What seems to be the disturbance?”

“Sparklehoof. My little griffin. He has become heroically stubborn.”

On a nearby ledge sat Sparklehoof, usually as fluffy as a newly formed cloud, today puffed like a miniature lion, tiny eagle’s beak pointed in defiance at a single glistening dewdrop.

“He refuses to fly down,” Nessa said. “He has declared a quest to conquer the Mighty Dewdrop of Dawn. Destiny. Bravest griffin in Aeridor.”

Merryshins peered. A creature known for chasing butterflies and napping in sunbeams. A dewdrop. Rather anticlimactic.

“He usually adores swooping,” Nessa fretted, stroking the griffin, who remained unmoving. “I have tried coaxing, tickling the ear tufts, even his favourite sky-berries. He stares at that dewdrop, determined.”

A familiar tug in Merryshins’ chest: the derailment of a peaceful day. He could have turned back to the rock. He looked at Nessa’s plea, then at the ridiculous puffed stance facing a bead of water, and a different feeling stirred: a quiet competitive streak. A wish to prove that an ordinary ogre could be a bit cleverer than a determined dewdrop. Wit, perhaps, instead of muscle.

“Perhaps Sparklehoof requires a more strategic approach,” he said. “A logical one.”

Nessa brightened. “You’ll help.”

“I believe this griffin needs to be out-stubborned. With the sharpest weapon I possess: my mind.”

They approached the ledge. Sparklehoof puffed further and let out a tiny fierce squawk, more indignant than fearsome.

“Greetings, brave Sparklehoof,” Merryshins said, gentle as moss on rock. “A noble quest. The fearsome dewdrop. Mighty not in size, but in unpredictability.”

Sparklehoof nodded sagely, chest out. He approved of this understanding.

“But,” Merryshins continued, confidential, “have you considered the danger? This dewdrop is infamous for sudden evaporation. One moment a shimmering orb of challenge. The next: gone. The bravest griffin left bewildered, without a trophy. A truly undignified end.”

Sparklehoof tilted his head. Uncertainty flickered. He had not considered the anticlimax of victory.

“And what if it is too mighty?” Nessa chimed, light as cloud. “What if vanquishing it unleashes a torrent that drenches you from beak to tail? Dripping and miserable is not triumphant.”

Sparklehoof took a step back. Posture deflated a fraction. The dewdrop now held a certain unpredictable menace.

Merryshins gestured with a large green hand. “The only truly safe conquest is from a distance. From the cozy confines of your mother’s nest, where you may observe its fate without personal risk. A strategic retreat is often wise.”

The griffin pondered. Dewdrop. Kindly ogre face. Nessa’s reassuring smile. The determined glint softened. A questioning chirp.

“Precisely,” Merryshins chuckled, a pleasant rumble. “True bravery is not rushing headlong. Sometimes a dewdrop is simply a dewdrop, best admired from afar.”

With a hesitant chirp that seemed to concede the point, Sparklehoof unfurled his wings. A tentative hop, then another, then a small apologetic flutter into the air. He circled once, a miniature whirlwind, and landed on Nessa’s arm, nudging her cheek. The dewdrop still glistened, unconquered, and perhaps a little relieved.

Nessa laughed, hugging him. The griffin purred like a miniature engine. “You little adventurer. You had us worried. And you were brave to listen.” She turned to Merryshins. “You have a remarkable way with stubborn creatures.”

Warmth spread through him, a different warmth than the morning sun. Not the exhilarating rush of a grand heroic deed, not the cheers of a grateful kingdom. The quiet profound satisfaction of solving a puzzle, of using his mind to untangle a tricky problem, and yes, a small secret flicker of the competitive joy of having outwitted the situation. He looked out at the cloud-brushed kingdom, wind whispering through ancient stone towers. His day had not been entirely drama-free, as he had wished. It had been, in its own unique way, perfectly splendid. Sparklehoof nestled contentedly into Nessa’s embrace. Merryshins returned to his sun-warmed rock, which had kept his place, and watched pine shadows stripe the path after all. The dewdrop, later, evaporated on schedule, which was how you knew a quest could end without a trophy and still count. Nessa, flying home, called a thanks that the wind spirits might have claimed as their own. Merryshins, who had wanted ordinariness, found that out-stubborning a griffin was, in Aeridor, as ordinary as moss.
characters: Merryshins (ogre who wants one un-volunteered day), Nessa (an elf with a stubborn griffin)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
